procedural_history.originating_court: Special Judge (inferred from the text, as the appellant made a written application to the learned Special Judge)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated the 5th November, 1982 of the Allahabad High Court in Criminal Contempt Case No. 144/SL.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Allahabad initiated contempt proceedings, found the appellant guilty of having committed criminal contempt under Section 2(c)(1) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, after affording him full opportunity of hearing, and imposed a sentence of simple imprisonment for 1 week and a fine of Rs. 500/- (in default to undergo a further term of simple imprisonment for 1 week).
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed the High Court's decision to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the tendering of an apology is sufficient to set aside a conviction for criminal contempt of court.

facts: An advocate was convicted of criminal contempt by the High Court and sentenced to imprisonment and a fine.
The advocate appealed to the Supreme Court.
Initially, no apology was offered to the judge who was scandalized.
Only after the Supreme Court showed reluctance to hear the appeal on the sentence did the advocate ask for time to apologize.
He then tendered a written apology to the judge, stating he was doing so "as directed by the Him'ble Supreme Court."
law: The Supreme Court established that an apology is not a universal rule for setting aside a contempt conviction, but rather an exception.
The court's primary considerations are the maintenance of the independence of the judiciary and the morale of judges.
application: The Court characterized the advocate's apology as a mere "'paper' apology" where the sorrow "came from his pen, not from his heart."
The fact that the apology was only tendered after prompting from the Supreme Court and included the phrase "as directed by" the court indicated it was not sincere or voluntary.
The Court rejected what it called the "'slap-say sorry-and forget' school of thought," arguing that a formal, empty apology does not undo the harm caused by scandalizing a court.
The Court reasoned that if such apologies were routinely accepted, it would be "tantamount to issuing a 'licence' to scandalize courts and commit contempt of court with impunity."
It concluded that allowing the appellant to escape punishment on the basis of this insincere apology would damage the independence of the judiciary and the morale of judges.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the mere tendering of an apology, especially one that is insincere and offered only under compulsion, is not sufficient to set aside a conviction for criminal contempt. The Court affirmed the sentence, stating that protecting the judiciary's independence and morale demanded that the appellant not escape with impunity.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the tendering of an apology is sufficient to set aside a conviction for criminal contempt of court.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that his tendering of an apology should be sufficient to escape punishment for the contempt of court.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that a mere apology does not wipe out the mischief of the contempt, and that considerations for maintaining the independence of the judiciary and the morale of judges demand that the appellant not escape with impunity.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An apology tendered for contempt of court does not automatically purge the contempt, as accepting such apologies as a rule, rather than an exception, would undermine the independence of the judiciary and be tantamount to issuing a license to scandalize courts with impunity.
obiter: If a Judge who renders a decision that is resented by a litigant were to be exposed to risk, it would sound the death knell of the judicial institution.
The contempt jurisdiction has to be exercised very sparingly and with circumspection.
A line has to be drawn somewhere, some day, by someone.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that considerations regarding the maintenance of the independence of the judiciary and the morale of judges demand that the appellant not be allowed to escape with impunity on the mere tendering of an apology. The court held that an apology does not wipe out the mischief of the contempt, and to accept it as a rule would be tantamount to issuing a 'licence' to scandalize courts and commit contempt with impunity.
legal_tests_applied: The court did not apply a formal, named legal test but operated on the principle that the contempt jurisdiction must be exercised very sparingly and with circumspection.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's tendering of an apology was deemed insufficient because it does not wipe out the mischief of the contempt committed.

The court reasoned that if such an apology were to be accepted as a rule, and not as an exception, it would virtually be tantamount to issuing a 'licence' to scandalize courts and commit contempt of court with impunity.
why_respondent_won: The court accepted that the maintenance of the independence of the judiciary and the morale of judges required that the appellant not escape punishment.
The court was impelled to act, rather than merely sermonize, because a line had to be drawn to protect the institution of the judiciary from intimidation.
The court refused to adopt an attitude of unmerited leniency at the cost of principle and at the expense of the judge who had been scandalized.
policy_considerations: If a judge rendering a decision that is resented by a litigant or lawyer were to expose him to such risk, it would sound the death knell of the institution.
The day must be dreaded when a Judge cannot work with independence by reason of the fear that a disgruntled member of the Bar can publicly humiliate him and heap disgrace on him with impunity.

No sitting Judge will feel free to decide any matter as per the dictates of his conscience on account of the fear of being scandalized and persecuted by an Advocate who does not mind making reckless allegations.

If this situation were to be countenanced, advocates who can cow down the Judges and make them fall in line with their wishes by threats of character assassination and persecution will be preferred by litigants over advocates who are mindful of professional ethics.
Institutional perspective demands that considerations of populism are not allowed to obstruct the path of duty.
